narration: The Living Fire: The Stomp Dance of the Eastern Woodlands
This is Stomp dance. Pre-colonial to present.
on_screen: Title card: Stomp dance · United States · Pre-colonial to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The stomp dance is an Eastern Woodland tradition practiced by tribes such as the Muscogee, Cherokee, and Seminole.

Its structure is centered on the Square Ground, a space designed with arbors and a central fire, which has been maintained across generations, particularly in Oklahoma and the southeastern United States.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a religious ceremony involving fasting, medicine, and communal prayer.
It is held throughout the night until dawn.
It serves as a spiritual and physical benefit to the community and is a core element of tribal identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Participants form a continuous spiral moving counterclockwise around a central fire.
The movement consists of deliberate stomping steps.
Women, who wear shell shakers on their legs, lead the rhythm immediately behind the male song leader, while other participants follow in alternating male-female order.
Watch for Stomp and shuffle.

Formation: Continuous counterclockwise spiral around a central fire.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is characterized by call-and-response singing in native languages.
Instruments include handheld rattles made from box turtle shells, gourds, or coconuts, and leg shakers made from turtle shells or condensed milk cans.
Listen for the box turtle shell rattles, gourd rattles, coconut rattles, turtle shell leg shakers.
The sound is defined by the rhythmic, metallic or organic clatter of leg shakers against the steady, stomping footsteps of the dancers, layered over male call-and-response vocals.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear casual but respectful attire, often including ribbon shirts.
Women wear full cotton skirts, sometimes featuring ribbonwork.
The setting is the Square Ground, an outdoor ceremonial space with a central fire and surrounding clan-houses or camps.
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Redbird Smith, a leader in the Cherokee traditionalist revival; Lydia Sam, a Natchez-Cherokee traditionalist who introduced the use of tin can shackles.

Variations exist between tribes, such as the Chickasaw maintaining grounds without medicine due to historical assimilation, and the Caddo, Delaware, and Choctaw maintaining secular or social versions.
The dance is a continuous tradition of the Eastern Woodland peoples, with specific ceremonial grounds serving as the primary sites of transmission.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The stomp dance is a religious ceremony. Photography is prohibited, and participants must adhere to strict rules regarding alcohol, drugs, and personal conduct. Outsiders should not attempt to record or participate without explicit invitation and guidance from the community.

narration: An exploration of the sacred, night-long ritual that connects generations of Eastern Woodland tribes to their ancestors and the earth.
